description: The Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur, also known as the Big Temple or Brihadeeswarar Temple, is a Hindu temple dedicated to Shiva. It was built by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I in the early 11th century CE, with inscriptions marking its completion around 1010 CE. The temple is part of the UNESCO World Heritage property 'Great Living Chola Temples'. Its vimana, the tower above the sanctum, rises to about 66 metres and is among the tallest temple towers of its period, built from interlocking granite blocks without mortar. The temple complex also houses a massive Nandi statue and preserves Chola-era inscriptions and paintings.
history: Granite for the Brihadisvara Temple was not available locally and had to be transported from quarries roughly 50 kilometres away. The temple's inscriptions record details of its endowments, administration, and the artisans involved in its construction. The temple remains in active worship today, which is reflected in its inclusion among the 'Great Living Chola Temples'.

sources.title: Great Living Chola Temples

description: The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram) on the Coromandel Coast of Tamil Nadu is part of the UNESCO World Heritage property 'Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram'. It was built in the 8th century CE during the reign of the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, also known as Rajasimha. It is one of the earliest structural stone temples in South India, meaning it was built from assembled stone blocks rather than being carved out of living rock. The temple complex faces the Bay of Bengal and includes shrines dedicated to Shiva.
history: Located directly on the seashore, the Shore Temple has endured centuries of exposure to wind and salt spray from the Bay of Bengal. Mahabalipuram was a major port city of the Pallava dynasty, and its monuments include chariot-shaped rathas, cave sanctuaries, and giant open-air reliefs such as the Descent of the Ganges, reflecting Pallava art and religion.

sources.title: Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram

description: The Sun Temple at Konark, Odisha, is a UNESCO World Heritage property inscribed as 'Sun Temple, Konârak'. It was built in the 13th century CE, around 1250, during the reign of King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. Dedicated to Surya, the Hindu Sun god, the temple was conceived as a colossal stone chariot with 24 intricately carved wheels and seven horses, symbolizing the Sun's journey across the sky. It is a masterpiece of Kalinga architecture.
history: The Konark temple is renowned for its elaborate stone sculpture, including figures and decorative motifs covering its walls. Much of the main temple structure has fallen into ruin over the centuries, while the audience hall, known as the jagamohana, remains standing. The site continues to be associated with the worship of Surya and with the cultural heritage of Odisha.

description: The Meenakshi Amman Temple in Madurai, Tamil Nadu, is a historic Hindu temple dedicated to the goddess Meenakshi (a form of Parvati) and her consort Sundareswarar (a form of Shiva). The temple complex is one of the most important pilgrimage sites in South India and is renowned for its towering gopurams (gateway towers) covered in thousands of colourful sculpted figures. The present structure largely dates to the 16th–17th century CE under the Nayaka dynasty, though the temple's origins are older. It is a major example of Dravidian architecture.
history: The Meenakshi Temple's thousand-pillared hall and its massive gopurams are defining features of Dravidian temple architecture. The annual Meenakshi Thirukalyanam festival celebrates the divine marriage of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar and draws hundreds of thousands of devotees. The temple complex is laid out in concentric square enclosures and sits at the heart of the ancient city of Madurai.

description: The Jagannath Temple in Puri, Odisha, is one of the Char Dham pilgrimage sites sacred to Hindus. Dedicated to Jagannath (a form of Krishna/Vishnu), the temple was rebuilt in the 12th century CE by King Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. The temple is famous for its annual Rath Yatra (chariot festival), during which the deities are placed on enormous wooden chariots and pulled through the streets by devotees.
history: The Jagannath Temple follows Kalinga architectural style, with a tall curvilinear spire (deula) over the sanctum. The temple kitchen is reputed to be among the largest in the world, preparing the Mahaprasad offering cooked in earthen pots over wood fire. The temple remains in active worship and is an important centre of Odia culture and heritage. The Rath Yatra or chariot festival at the Jagannath Temple in Puri is one of the largest and oldest Hindu festivals. During the festival, the deities Jagannath, Balabhadra, and Subhadra are taken from the temple in enormous wooden chariots to the Gundicha Temple, about three kilometres away, where they remain for several days before returning. The festival attracts millions of devotees and is a significant expression of Odia religious and cultural heritage.

description: The Kashi Vishwanath Temple in Varanasi (Kashi), Uttar Pradesh, is one of the most famous Hindu temples dedicated to Shiva. Located on the western bank of the Ganges River, Varanasi is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and is considered a sacred city in Hinduism. The present temple structure was rebuilt in the 18th century CE by Queen Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore, though a temple on this site is much older.
history: The Kashi Vishwanath Temple's spire is gold-plated, and the temple complex includes smaller shrines and the Jnana Vapi (Wisdom Well). Varanasi's ghats along the Ganges and its temples make the city a major pilgrimage centre. The temple is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, considered especially sacred shrines of Shiva.
